excerpt: Why rollovers happen, the injuries they cause, and who may be liable — other drivers, vehicle makers, or road authorities — in Georgia and South Carolina.
keyTakeaways: Rollover crashes are among the most violent vehicle accidents, often caused by top-heavy SUVs, overcorrection, tire blowouts, or defective vehicle design. Occupants suffer traumatic brain injuries, spinal cord damage, ejection injuries, and crush injuries. Liability may fall on other drivers, vehicle manufacturers, or government entities responsible for road conditions. Georgia bars recovery at 50% or more fault (O.C.G.A. SS 51-12-33) and allows two years to file (O.C.G.A. SS 9-3-33), while South Carolina bars recovery at 51% fault and allows three years (S.C. Code SS 15-3-530).

faqs.question: What makes rollover crashes so dangerous?
faqs.answer: Rollover crashes subject occupants to violent multi-directional forces — throwing them sideways, upward, and downward in rapid succession. Occupants strike the roof, doors, windows, and dashboard repeatedly. If the roof crushes inward, survival space is reduced. Unbelted occupants face ejection, which increases the fatality risk by roughly 8 times according to NHTSA.

faqs.question: Who can be held liable for a rollover crash?
faqs.answer: Depending on the circumstances, liable parties may include another driver who caused the collision, the vehicle manufacturer if a design defect made the vehicle prone to rolling over or the roof collapsed, a tire manufacturer if a blowout triggered the rollover, a government entity if a road defect or missing guardrail contributed, or a trucking company if improper loading or driver fatigue was involved.

faqs.question: Can I still recover compensation if I was not wearing a seatbelt?
faqs.answer: Yes, in both states — but the rules now differ sharply. In Georgia, Senate Bill 68 revised O.C.G.A. § 40-8-76.1(d) effective April 21, 2025, so evidence that you were not wearing a seatbelt may be admitted on negligence, comparative negligence, causation, assumption of risk, or apportionment of fault, and may diminish your recovery. Georgia sets no fixed percentage reduction — the finder of fact apportions fault, and the court still weighs admissibility under O.C.G.A. § 24-4-403. In South Carolina the reverse applies: Under S.C. Code § 56-5-6540(C), a seatbelt violation is not negligence per se or contributory negligence and is not admissible as evidence in a civil action. In neither state does going unbelted bar your claim, and you remain entitled to compensation for injuries caused by another party's negligence.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a lawsuit after a rollover crash?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, the statute of limitations for personal injury is 2 years from the date of injury (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, it is 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Claims involving government entities may require notice much sooner — as early as 6 months to 1 year depending on the jurisdiction.

faqs.question: Are SUVs and trucks more likely to roll over?
faqs.answer: Yes. Vehicles with a higher center of gravity — including SUVs, pickup trucks, and vans — are significantly more prone to rollovers than sedans. However, any vehicle can roll over under the right circumstances, especially at high speed, during sharp turns, or after striking a curb, guardrail, or soft shoulder.

faqs.question: What damages can I recover after a rollover crash?
faqs.answer: You may recover economic damages (medical expenses, lost wages, future treatment costs, property damage), non-economic damages (pain and suffering, emotional distress, loss of enjoyment of life, disfigurement), and in cases involving extreme recklessness or defective products, punitive damages. If a loved one was killed, surviving family members may file a wrongful death claim.
